thread_title: S. rosea Southern Baldwin Co, AL
breadcrumb: S. rosea Southern Baldwin Co, AL

posts.body_html:
The AF luteola we have in cultivation today originally came from this population in Southern Baldwin Co, AL. The population as a whole is very diverse, and overall seems to be more disease resistant than any other roseas we have in the collection from various different counties. Vigor-wise, it grows just as fast as any other rosea population, and many plants seem to exhibit excellent green and red color contrasts on newly opened traps. However, once the leaf has fully matured, many clones seem to turn solid pink or reddish, but it's still too early to tell if that's the case for every single plant.

Some photos, taken 6/20/16. This color combo in the photo below is what I'm talking about:













Some are over-crowded in community trays hence the greener color:

posts.body_html: another yellow-ish clone! pics taken 11/30/22:

Check out this yellow clone! These are all traps from last year's growth, they haven't done much this season yet besides flower! Everything is way behind this year, probably because it's been unseasonably cool and we've had extended rains that usually peter out by the end of March, but it was still raining as of this morning! pics taken 5/5/23:


How do I know this yellow coloration as a genetic component to it? Because under exactly identical conditions, other clones are red (see plant to the left as an example)


flowers are normal colored for roseas, although I have to admit, they're a bit tall now that I think of it. Roseas tend to have shorter flower stalks, but that's not always the case:
